title: Which of these four statements are always or never true?
description: Four statements about multiples, sums, digits and an expression with brackets are each tested with letters. Three always hold and the last never does, because it always leaves eight over when divided by twelve. The method is the same as the examples in the book on always, sometimes and never true.
teaching_notes: One idea: write each statement with letters and take out the factor that decides it, or open the brackets and see what is left over. Watch for students who try a few numbers and call a statement always true or never true without showing why.

video_script.why: A learner writes four statements with letters, takes out a factor or opens brackets, and decides whether each is always, sometimes or never true.
video_script.substitution: the book's own four statements about multiples, three even numbers in a row, swapped digits, and 8(7b - 3) - 4(11b + 1)
video_script.anchor: four statement cards, each with letters and a factor taken out, as in the book
video_script.payoff_line: The first three statements are always true. The fourth statement is never true.

final_answer.spoken: the first three statements are always true, and the fourth statement is never true

maths_rules: (i) 6a x 3b = 18ab = 9 x 2ab: always a multiple of 9
(ii) three even numbers in a row 2n, 2n + 2, 2n + 4: sum 6n + 6 = 6(n + 1): always divisible by 6
(iii) abcdef and badcef have the same digits, so the same digit sum (test for 3) and the same last digit f (test for 2): always a multiple of 6
(iv) 8(7b - 3) - 4(11b + 1) = 56b - 24 - 44b - 4 = 12b - 28 = 12(b - 3) + 8: always leaves 8 over, never a multiple of 12
video_script.design: One idea: take out a factor, or open brackets and see what is left over. Assumes the examples on always, sometimes and never true, and the tests for two and three. The four statement cards stay on the board.

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about four statements on multiples.
<bookmark mark='same'/>We will solve it the same way as the examples in your book.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is each statement always true, sometimes true, or never true?

beats.on_screen: the four statement cards stay on the board while the child thinks

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: always: fits every time. never: fails every time. letters stand for every number at once

marks.always: the always and never boxes light up with their meaning
marks.letters: a letter card glows beside a row of many numbers

narration: <bookmark mark='always'/>A statement is always true if it fits every number. It is never true if it fails for every number.
<bookmark mark='letters'/>A letter stands for every number at once, so it can test them all.

beats.on_screen: Given: four statements about multiples, three even numbers in a row, digits, and an expression with brackets

marks.given: the four statements are written one under the other

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, there are four statements about multiples, digits and an expression.

beats.on_screen: To find: always, sometimes or never true, for each statement
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find if each one is always, sometimes or never true.

marks.state: the statement about a multiple of six multiplied by a multiple of three is written
marks.write: six eigh times three b becomes eighteen eigh b, then nine times two eigh b

narration: <bookmark mark='state'/>Step one, a multiple of six multiplied by a multiple of three is a multiple of nine.
<bookmark mark='write'/>Six eigh times three b is eighteen eigh b, which is nine times two eigh b. It is always true.

marks.state: three even numbers in a row are written as two n, two n plus two and two n plus four
marks.sum: the sum becomes six n plus six, then six times a bracket

narration: <bookmark mark='state'/>Step two, take three even numbers in a row. They are two n, two n plus two, and two n plus four.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Their sum is six n plus six, which is six times the bracket n plus one. It is always true.

beats.on_screen: (iii) abcdef and badcef: same digits, same digit sum, same last digit f: always true

marks.swap: the digits eigh and b swap places, and c and d swap places
marks.three: the digit sum is marked the same, so the test for three still passes
marks.two: the last digit f is marked the same, so the test for two still passes

narration: <bookmark mark='swap'/>Step three, swap the digits in pairs. The new number b eigh d c e f has the same digits as before.
<bookmark mark='three'/>The digit sum is the same, so the test for three still passes.
<bookmark mark='two'/>The last digit f is the same, so the test for two still passes. It is always true.

marks.state: the expression with brackets is written
marks.open: the brackets are opened to fifty six b minus twenty four minus forty four b minus four
marks.tidy: the terms are tidied to twelve b minus twenty eight
marks.left: twelve times the bracket b minus three, plus eight appears, with eight left over

narration: <bookmark mark='state'/>Step four, take the expression. Eight times the bracket seven b minus three, take away four times the bracket eleven b plus one.
<bookmark mark='open'/>Open the brackets. That gives fifty six b minus twenty four, minus forty four b, minus four.
<bookmark mark='tidy'/>Tidy it to twelve b minus twenty eight.
<bookmark mark='left'/>That is twelve times the bracket b minus three, plus eight. It always leaves eight over, so it is never a multiple of twelve.

marks.first: six times three shows eighteen, nine times two
marks.second: four plus six plus eight shows eighteen, six times three
marks.third: b as four gives two hundred minus one hundred and eighty, which is twenty, and twenty is twelve plus eight

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step five, put numbers back to check. Six times three is eighteen, which is nine times two.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Four plus six plus eight is eighteen, which is six times three.
<bookmark mark='third'/>With b as four, the expression gives two hundred minus one hundred and eighty, which is twenty. Twenty is twelve plus eight.

marks.ans: the answer line is boxed and the four cards slide into the boxes

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The first three statements are always true. The fourth statement is never true.
